fixes.explanation: That's the one, friend. The Teacher says, “The fool folds his hands and consumes his own flesh.” I'm picturing somebody leaning back with those folded hands. It's a sharp little line, and it sits right next to all that envy-driven labor, so the Teacher has both sides of the picture covered.

Nice try, friend, and I'd love to hand the wise man that line too. But the text says “The fool folds his hands and consumes his own flesh.” (Ecclesiastes 4:5). The Teacher gives it to the fool, and the wise man just has to watch.

I get the guess, friend. But this verse doesn't mention a rich man. It says, “The fool folds his hands and consumes his own flesh.” The Teacher names the fool, and he doesn't say a word about what's in anybody's pockets.

That's right, friend. The Teacher says that though this man's labor has no end, “…his eyes are still not content with his wealth…” He has the wealth, and his eyes still aren't content with it. That's the part that makes it hard to watch.

That's the word, baker. The Teacher says, “This too is futile—a miserable task.” A man alone, working without end, asking, “For whom do I toil and bereave my soul of enjoyment?” I think that's about as heavy as this passage gets, so I'll just say it plainly and move on.

Working nonstop can look wise from the outside, I'll give you that. But the Teacher says, “This too is futile—a miserable task.” He's looking at a man whose labor has no end and whose eyes are not content with his wealth. Wise isn't the word he picks.

Right on, friend. The Teacher says, “Two are better than one, because they have a good return for their labor.” Just before this, a lonely man asks, “For whom do I toil…” and this is the turn. Two people have a good return for their labor.

If only, right? But the Teacher says nothing like that. He says, “Two are better than one, because they have a good return for their labor.” The labor is still there, and the good return is what he says two have.
That's a gloomy pick, friend, and the Teacher doesn't go there. He says, “For if one falls down, his companion can lift him up…” The companion can lift him up. Taking a share isn't in the verse.

Walking past a fallen friend would be a rough kind of companion. The Teacher says the opposite: “For if one falls down, his companion can lift him up…” The companion can give him a hand up. Walking on isn't in the verse.

You got it, friend. The Teacher says, “Again, if two lie down together, they will keep warm; but how can one keep warm alone?” I think he asks it because the answer is already sitting there. My ovens keep the bakery toasty, but I'd still take company over a warm oven.

Forgotten is a strong word, friend, but it isn't in this verse. The Teacher says, “And though one may be overpowered, two can resist.” I've been overpowered by a lump of cold dough before, so I'm glad he brings up two. The word he uses is overpowered.

You got it, friend. The Teacher says, “Better is a poor but wise youth than an old but foolish king who no longer knows how to take a warning.” Wisdom beats the crown here. And notice what the text says about the king: he no longer knows how to take a warning.

Rich and foolish is a fun pairing, but that's not who the Teacher picks. He says, “Better is a poor but wise youth than an old but foolish king who no longer knows how to take a warning.” The better one is poor and wise. A prince isn't in this verse.

That one's False, friend. The Teacher says, “There is no limit to all the people who were before them. Yet the successor will not be celebrated by those who come even later.” So the people who come even later won't celebrate him. The verse says it plainly.

That's right, baker. The Teacher says, “Yet the successor will not be celebrated by those who come even later.” Even a youth who came from the prison to the kingship (Ecclesiastes 4:14) isn't celebrated by those who come even later. And then the Teacher says it again: “This too is futile and a pursuit of the wind.”
